sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Gaul was an ancient Celtic land. The name in modern use usually means a region of Europe bounded by the Rhine, the Alps, the Mediterranean, the Pyrenees, and the Atlantic and Channel shores. The term answers to Gallia Transalpina, that is Gaul beyond the Alps as seen from Rome. North of the Alps, Celts later moved south into the Po valley to form Cisalpine Gaul, and raids from there reached as far as the sack of Rome about 390 BCE. Caesar brought the northern peoples under Roman power and divided them into the Belgae, the Aquitani, and the Celtae or Galli. His campaigns ran from 58 to 51 BCE. The Greeks called these folk Celtoi, and the name links to a Celtic word for fierce spiritedness; in Old Irish gal means boldness. Much of what we know of the Gauls comes down through Roman accounts.
